\title{Inequality and Social Contests}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction }


\noindent
The relationship between inequality and status competitions remains
unclear. On one hand, status good are seen as social waste but both
empirical studies do suggest improvement of subjective welfare with
status goods. Whether status goods -that help maintain some subjective
decency in one's reference group contributes to economic action or
not is a question that is often reserved for sociology. Relying on
Weber and Goode on how consumption is social status may be linked
with economic activity, we consider the constraints of slower social
acclimatisation posed to an closed economy of firm and labour. Viewing
social networks as a constraint that firms must accommodate, we attempt
to answer how inequality may influence pressures on establishment
of social networks. 

\subsection{Closed Economy}

\noindent

The model assumes a closed economy in which all income circulates
between households and firms. Drawing on a Schumpeterian view, economic
growth arises in the model from continual introductions of new or
higher-quality goods. Workers supply labour and receive wages, and
these wages constitute the basis of domestic demand. Firms use the
revenue generated from this demand - either through investment financed
by household savings - to fund innovation. Successful innovation then
produces new varieties or improves existing products, generating the
next round of income. This circular flow of wages, consumption, and
innovation creates an endogenous engine of growth: consumption completes
one innovation cycle by returning income to firms, while investment
initiates the next by financing the search for new products. In long-run
equilibrium, firms are assumed to have already chosen an optimal allocation
of resources that sustains a steady stream of innovation and revenues.

Some investments flow back to the firm and some don't. A large part
of what doesn't flow back is not waste or efficiency loss but externality
costs to the firm. Education and training costs - where firms also
participate - are different from slow acclimatisation costs that are
spent on building social networks - maintaining notions of decency
imposed by differential social norms.

The model for endogenous growth economy uses a notion of a socio-economic class by accommodating two mobility mechanisms - one through upskilling and another through a social lottery. While the former reflects the systematic skill-based organisation of labour market, the latter represents connections-driven growth of the employee. It is assumed that the average growth of a participant of the economy involves hedging one's bets in both the mechanisms. 

\section{Model}

\noindent

An essential feature of the model for agent's dual purposes of status rewards through social competitions and economic success is that the rewards through social networks are outside the firm's direct influence. In other words, not all factors that influence labour sorting criteria are under firm's control. The job search costs for workers, or influence of social networks are social constraints that the firm is obliged to work around. Since the firm benefits from higher wage income through innovation and revenue , the costs of upskilling do flow back to the firm - unlike the costs of building social connections (encompassing  slow-categorisation) that do not flow back to the firm. 

We discuss a simple microeconomic formulation of above endogenous model and then provide a stylised macroeconomic model based on the model dynamics implied by the microeconomic formulation.

\subsection{Microeconomic formulation}

\noindent


In the microeconomic formulation of the endoegnous growth economy, the stratified labour is represented as fixed ladder of jobs occupied by workers at any given point in time. Each position in the ladder is associated with a distinct income level that is eventually set by the firm. Every worker holds exactly one job and the number of jobs does not change over time in the economy. While we assume no long-term unemployment, the workers in the economy face temporary job loss \footnote{The technological changes or internal reorganization that lead to such losses circusmscribe the creative destruction in endogenous growth economy.}. Upon the job-loss, the worker faces the choice to re-enter the job-market with costs of up-skilling and play a lottery to swap the current position with someone else in the job-market.

In other words, a displaced worker can return to the previous job by investing in the skills or certifications required to perform it. Since higher-ranked jobs with higher-income require greater skill, the upward move requires substantial retraining costs. The retraining costs are forgone by the worker in accepting lower-ranked jobs. Mobility thus occurs through three mechanisms i) voluntary movement down the ladder ii) costly investment to move upward iii) or a lottery for positions among other workers.

The model captures these possibilities with the three choices. The worker may  (i) swap her job with a lower-ranked worker who is willing to acquire the skills necessary to move up (therefore paying the price to move up) (ii) pay the skill cost required to claim a higher-ranked position from someone willing to step down, or (iii) pay a fixed cost that provides mobility with some risk (social lottery). Such options reflect different mechanisms of job mobility - training, competition, and luck.

The higher-income jobs involve greater training requirements (factoring in a longer search time and other costs arising out of short-term unemployment) and therefore a higher cost of acquiring such positions. But the preferences for risk also varies across income positions. In the current model, risk of income loss increases with higher income-levels in absolute terms. In other words, the workers in high-skill, high-income positions face greater absolute losses when displaced. All workers have the same preferences, they all exhibit the well-known risk-aversion for small gains and a higher risk-taking at higher loss levels - a behaviour that the model capture with an S-shaped Friedman-Savage utility for the worker.

A worker has income $m_i$ - but she may go into a role that $m_{k}$ so long as she pays a transition-cost $C(m_i,m_{k})$ which is a power-cost-function. For $\forall {k<i}$,  we have $C(m_i,m_{k})=0$ i.e. no cost is paid for moving down from a position of high-skill to low-skill. The income-levels themselves are specified with a single-paramter $a$ in the pareto income list $ x_0  (1 - i)^{-1 / a}$ for $1 \le i \le N$.  Higher $\gamma$ corresponds to higher costs-charged by the firm and a higher $a$ corresponds to higher-stakes through income levels. Higher costs discourage mobility and higher stakes encourage bets. If revenue in every period is fixed then stakes can be raised only by using a lottery. In a full-scale model, there is a fixed number of transititions every period so that a lottery is activated only when cost-based transactions aren't feasible. In a reduced-model, we consider that the worker either pays cost-of-upskill or tries to use the lottery. The latter costs justify social alignment (contest) while the former justifies firm's investments.


Lottery matters more to the lower paid worker - esp when it's low-value. The higher risk seeking at low wealth levels through the S-shaped utility function also implies that in the long-term equilibrium, the higher-rank workers would prefer the downgrade while the low-rank workers may prefer the lottery. 



Another dynamic implied by the above mobility in a closed economy is that the pool for swapping gets limited with higher ranks. In other words, the more a worker upskills oneself, the harder it becomes for the worker to move up (as the swap pool gets limited). The long-term transition-probability is therefore determined by the costs of moving up the ladder.
